institutionName: Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Toulouse (Sciences Po)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere where I could take classes in French because I wanted to learn French while abroad. Of the three French cities I could go to (Paris, Lyon, Toulouse), Toulouse was the smallest, the most charming, and seemed like the easiest place to learn French. I also wanted a very "liveable" city rather than a tourist destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It has been a very chill enjoyable experience. Lots of sweet people, and going to cafes and bars and having a good time, but nothing "wild" like a lot of travelling or partying.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Once there, it is pretty easy to get the information. If you take the French track, you start out with a week with French classes where you get to know the other internationals on French track, and during the week they host a preparatory information meeting for all internationals. It is possible to write an email and ask question or, even easier, just drop by the international office and talk to them. The part that can be hard (if you have mandatory classes at the sending university that you have to replace) is to get the necessary information in advance.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: French class, information meeting, emails with information. They send out the email with information about where to find more information, for example where to find the "welcome desk".

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I applied for rooms in shared appartments. I didn't want to live in CROUS because having my own room and not getting to know the other people living there seemed a little lonely. I applied for a LOT of apartments on
lacartedescolocs.fr
and got a room in an apartment with three other girls. So it did take more work than a CROUS room, but was a better option for me. It wasn't a very social apartment, and I think the "colocations" most often aren't very social, but still nice and liveable. Rent was 500€, but I got about 100€ of CAF for two of the months.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Both will be fine. Also the city isn't that big, so even if you don't live in the center, it'll be fine. I lived somewhere Minimes and Negreneys and just biked to school.

Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to send a bunch of documents, including proof of language level, but it isn't that complicated.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can email the international office and ask questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got exactly the classes I wanted. You start out with a one/two week period where you try out the classes before you do the final registration, which is very helpful. They are pretty flexible with which French classes internationals take. When taking “normal” classes in French with the French students, there is a formal limit of five international students, but if the teacher doesn't mind having more, they don't enforce it.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Definitely try out a lot of courses before deciding to get an idea of what you like.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In general, it is lower than in Copenhagen. Classes are way less theoretical and to a larger degree concern a specific topic. The hard part is taking French classes if it isn't your native language. But because the classes count for 5ECTS for internationals, and they are made to count 2/3ECTS for the normal students, the workload isn't too big.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Classes are way less interactive. Some of them (but definitely not all!) just consist of a teacher reading a document out loud. Instead of doing a combination of lectures + smaller classes, the classes are either or. They are more empiric and less theoretical. They are less (not at all) quantitative and more qualitative. They are more concerned about form (the French “dissertation”) and less about content.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Institutions politiques comparées, Sociologie des conflits, L'Europe du vote, Institutions européennes, Culture et civilisation françaises, Histoire de la pensée féministe.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Histoire de la pensée féministe was awesome but probably won't be available next year. Sociologie des conflits is really good cause you get an insight into some of the worlds biggest conflicts (eg. Israel-Palestine, Afghanistan) and the teacher is really good. L'Europe du vote was nice cause there was a bit of interaction – presentations about texts and then a little discussion after the presentations. Culture at civilisation françaises was very patriotic but also really good to just learn in general about the history of France, and the teacher is well prepared. Avoid Institutions européennes if you can, it is just a teacher reading a boring document out loud.
In general see if you can do some "seminaires" - it's smaller classes on the master which are more fun than the big lecture classes.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing big.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Lunch and dinner could be cheap because we often ate at the publicly funded university restaurant (Resto U' Arsenal) where you can get a filling meal for lunch/dinner for 3,30€. French veggies were surprisingly expensive. A tip for transportation if you wanna bike is (beside VeloToulouse which is a really good system) to rent a bike at Maisondevelo, where it costs 10€ per month.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A whole bunch of associations. If you're fast you can sign up for a sport at UT Capitole. Sometimes the university hosts an event, eg. an informational election night the night of the American presidential election. But you have to be proactive and search it out.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sign up for associations to get to know french people. Go hiking in the Pyrenees, it's not that far – there are some cheap options like going with ESN or with a sports association at UT Capitole. You can also go yourself by train or BlaBlaCar. You can also go visit some of the cute smaller towns in the area, with well-preserved buildings from the Middle Ages and renaissance (like Albi, Carcassonne, Narbonne). Also in general, just use the city, there's lots of life and things to do – cafés, bars, the theater etc.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See above answer.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It is always gonna take a little while to settle in when moving to a different country. You have to figure out how to navigate in a country with another language and find new habits for things like cooking and getting around. But for the most part it didn't take more than a couple of weeks.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: If you wanna speak French with them, then sign up for lots of associations. You won't get to talk a lot to them in class so really the best place to get to know them is associations. Some of them don't work out or they meet very rarely so try to go to information meetings and events with multiple to see what you like and what works out. Not all the sports associations actually worked out, but dance and football seemed good. I liked the cultural association Posculture. Follow a lot of them on Instagram to see if they post events. However they mostly speak and share information in French so it's mostly for if you wanna learn french.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Speaking french. The non-interactive teaching style. Also they eat super late, so if you live in a colocation, you might also end up eating very late.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The culture for going out and enjoying life. There's lots of just sitting in cafes, drinking your coffee, doing your work. And lots of going out for beers.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Take initiatives so you get to know the other exchange students, don't stress out about having to “accomplish” anything specific with the stay, and remember to just enjoy it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you're on the french track, all your classes are gonna be with different people, making it a bit difficult to get to know people to begin with. So do some classes with the internationals so you meet up a couple times a week, and take initiative to get to know each other in the beginning.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning that I can do something that seemed impossible : studying in a language that I didn't speak very well to begin with.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: In the beginning it was tough getting used to the language, and the first two weeks it was really really hard for my head that everything was in French. Also, on the french track it can be a bit tough to not have a social "base" because all the classes are with different people, so again make sure to get to know some of the internationals in the same situation well.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
